lesson_title: Data Handling: from Survey Question to Honest Graph
hook_text: Eleven friends. Mean spending R35. Median R30. Same data, two different answers — and one of them is playing you.
clip_script: Eleven friends, weekly tuck-shop money, sorted: 10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 — and one big spender at 100. The mean: pool it all, R385, deal it out — R35 each. The median: stand them in a queue, tap the middle shoulder — R30. Why the fight? That R100. The mean shook hands with it — every rand joins the pot, so one lavish spender lifts the share-out. The median never met it — the queue's midpoint doesn't care how rich the last person is. Outliers in the data? Trust the median. That's why serious reports quote MEDIAN income, not mean. Now the graph trick. Two bars: R28 and R32. Open the axis at R25 and the R32 bar stands more than twice as tall — a R4 gap staged as a rout. Check where the axis starts, read the real numbers, say them out loud. And before any of it: who did you ask? Survey only your grade 11 circle and the whole school looks richer than it is. That's bias — and chance, not convenience, is the only fair chooser.
visual_style: Eleven learners in a queue holding rand amounts overhead, the R100 friend glowing as the mean slides up a number line while the median stands firm; a bar graph whose floor lifts to R25 and drops back to zero, the towering bar shrinking to honest size.
mood: Sceptical and empowering — the friend who teaches you to catch statistics misbehaving.
pacing: Playful through the queue and share-out, a snap of tension at the outlier, slowing to a deliberate reveal on the truncated axis.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never be fooled by an average or a graph again.
